case: State of Odisha and Others v. Dhanurdhar Champatiray
headline: A Writ Petition Remains Available Against a Section 37 Arbitration Order Despite the Bar on Second Appeal: Orissa High Court
summary: Rejecting the preliminary objection that nine writ petitions against District Judges' Section 37 appellate orders were an impermissible substitute for a barred second appeal, Justice B.P. Routray held that the High Court's constitutional jurisdiction under Articles 226 and 227 is not an appellate remedy and cannot be curtailed by the Arbitration Act's bar on second appeals, though such supervisory jurisdiction remain

case: J&K Economic Reconstruction Agency v. Rash Builders India — 2026 INSC 368
headline: Seat of Arbitration Confers Exclusive Jurisdiction — Venue Is Merely a Convenient Location
summary: The Supreme Court reaffirmed that the seat of arbitration is the juridical home of the arbitration, fixing the curial law and the court with exclusive supervisory jurisdiction once designated by the parties' agreement — to the exclusion of every other court, even one where part of the cause of action arose. The venue, by contrast, is only a geographical convenience and does not confer, alter, or determine jurisdictio

case: Jan De Nul Dredging India Pvt. Ltd. v. Tuticorin Port Trust
headline: Section 37 Appellate Scrutiny Cannot Exceed the Grounds Available Under Section 34
summary: The Supreme Court held that jurisdiction under Section 37 mirrors that under Section 34 — courts hearing a Section 37 appeal do not sit as ordinary appellate courts and must not interfere with an award merely because an alternative view is possible. The appellate court's role is confined to verifying whether the Section 34 court acted within, exceeded, or failed to exercise its conferred powers.

case: Glencore International AG v. Shree Ganesh Metals — 2025 SCC OnLine SC 1815
headline: Unsigned Arbitration Agreement Is Binding if Parties Act on It Through Correspondence and Conduct
summary: The Supreme Court held that parties who negotiated a contract through email and then acted on its terms — including an embedded arbitration clause — were bound by that clause even though the contract was never formally signed. The exchange of electronic correspondence and the parties' conduct evidenced acceptance of the contract terms including the arbitration agreement.

case: ASF Buildtech Pvt. Ltd. v. Shapoorji Pallonji — 2025 INSC 616
headline: Arbitral Tribunal Can Itself Implead a Non-Signatory Under the Group of Companies Doctrine
summary: The Supreme Court held that an arbitral tribunal has the inherent power to implead a non-signatory to arbitration proceedings by applying the Group of Companies doctrine — based on common control, management overlap, and integrated contract performance within a corporate group. This power is exercisable by the tribunal without requiring a fresh court referral under Section 11.

case: Tata Steel v. Raj Kumar Banerjee — 2025 SCC OnLine SC 1042
headline: IBC Section 61(2): NCLAT Has No Jurisdiction to Condone Delay Beyond the 45-Day Outer Limit
summary: The Supreme Court set aside an NCLAT order that had permitted an appeal to be filed 46 days after the NCLT order — one day beyond the outer limit. The Court held that Section 61(2) of the IBC prescribes a mandatory outer limit of 45 days (30 + 15) for filing appeals. The NCLAT, being a creature of statute, cannot assume equitable or inherent jurisdiction to override this express legislative limit. The CIRP of Rohit F

case: Gayatri Balasamy v. ISG Novasoft Technologies — 2025 INSC 1057
headline: Constitution Bench Holds: Courts Have Limited Power to Modify Arbitral Awards Under Sections 34 & 37
summary: A five-judge bench by a 4:1 majority, authored by CJI Sanjiv Khanna, held that courts have a limited inherent power to modify arbitral awards under Sections 34 and 37 of the Arbitration Act. Modification is permissible to: sever legally separable invalid portions; correct obvious clerical, typographical, or computational errors; and adjust post-award interest rates in appropriate cases. The majority applied the princ

case: Adavya Projects v. M/s Vishal Structurals — 2025 INSC 507
headline: Whether a Non-Signatory Is Bound by an Arbitration Agreement Is for the Tribunal to Decide Conclusively
summary: The Supreme Court clarified the Group of Companies doctrine: the referral court under Sections 8 and 11 makes only a prima facie finding on whether a non-signatory is involved — it is left to the arbitral tribunal to conclusively decide whether the non-signatory is bound by the arbitration agreement. Non-joinder at the Section 11 stage does not prevent later impleadment by the tribunal.

case: M/s Ferro Concrete Construction v. State of Rajasthan — 2025 INSC 429
headline: Contractual Bar on Interest Operates Differently Under the 1996 Arbitration Act vs. 1940 Act
summary: The Supreme Court restored an arbitrator's discretion to award pendente lite interest, holding that a general 'no interest' clause in a contract does not prevent an arbitrator under the 1996 Act from awarding interest unless the contract expressly prohibits it. The court awarded 9% pendente lite interest, distinguishing the stricter position under the 1940 Act.

case: Disortho S.A.S. v. Meril Life Sciences — 2025 INSC 352
headline: Venue of Arbitration Does Not Determine the Law Governing the Arbitration Agreement
summary: The Supreme Court held that the contract must be read as a whole. Where the contract designated Colombian law for arbitration proceedings but Indian law as the lex contractus, Indian courts retained supervisory jurisdiction. The venue of arbitration (Bogotá) did not determine the governing law of the arbitration agreement. In the absence of an express choice, the lex contractus ordinarily governs the arbitration agre

case: M/s C&C Constructions v. IRCON International — 2025 INSC 138
headline: Section 37 Appellate Jurisdiction Cannot Exceed the Scope Prescribed Under Section 34
summary: The Supreme Court clarified that the appellate jurisdiction under Section 37 of the Arbitration Act is narrowly circumscribed and cannot exceed the limits under Section 34. An appellate court under Section 37 cannot independently assess the merits of an award; it is confined to examining whether the court below acted within Section 34's bounds.

case: Serosoft Solutions v. Dexter Capital Advisors — 2025 INSC 26
headline: HC Writ Interference With Arbitral Orders Requires Perversity Staring on the Face of the Record
summary: The Supreme Court held that interference by High Courts under Arts. 226/227 with arbitral tribunal orders is permissible only where the order is completely perverse and that perversity is evident on the face of the record. The Court emphasised that High Courts must actively discourage satellite litigation that disrupts the arbitral process — excessive judicial intervention is antithetical to arbitration's efficiency

case: GVV Constructions Pvt. Ltd. v. Union of India & Ors.
headline: Whether a Claim Falls Within an 'Excepted Matters' Clause Is for the Arbitral Tribunal, Not a Section 11 Court
summary: The Supreme Court held that whether a particular claim in a works contract is covered by, or falls outside, an "excepted matters" clause is a question squarely within the competence of the Arbitral Tribunal under Section 16 — not one for a court exercising appointment-stage jurisdiction under Section 11. The Court also held that a writ appellate court cannot pre-determine arbitral jurisdiction or restrict a tribunal'

case: C. Velusamy v. K. Indhera
headline: A Tribunal's Mandate Can Still Be Extended Under Section 29A Even After an Award Is Passed Post-Expiry: Supreme Court
summary: A Bench of Justices Pamidighantam Sri Narasimha and Atul S. Chandurkar held that an application under Section 29A(5) of the Arbitration and Conciliation Act, 1996 to extend an arbitral tribunal's mandate is maintainable even after expiry of the statutory time limit under Sections 29A(1) and (3), and even where an award has already been rendered during the interim period. The Court noted that an award passed after the

case: In Re: Cartelisation in the Supply of Tyres to Himachal Pradesh Road Transport Corporation
headline: CCI Fines Tyre Dealers for Bid Rigging, but Exonerates the Manufacturers Behind Them
summary: Examining a 2013 Himachal Pradesh Road Transport Corporation tyre tender, the CCI found that two authorised dealers of JK Tyre and CEAT had exchanged commercially sensitive bid-price information by email before submission, with their quoted prices matching to the second decimal place, in contravention of Section 3(3)(d) of the Competition Act, 2002. It imposed modest penalties on the dealers but exonerated the tyre m

case: M/s Levitate Mobile Technologies Pvt. Ltd. v. M/s Standard Chartered Bank & Anr.
headline: Commercial Courts Act Is Meant for Expediency — Voluminous Evidence Cannot Dilute Its Rigours
summary: The Supreme Court held that the Commercial Courts Act, 2015 exists to secure speedy disposal of high-value commercial disputes, and that a litigant cannot resist timely production of evidence merely by pleading that the record is voluminous. The Court read this squarely into the summary and case-management procedures the Act builds on top of the ordinary CPC.

case: Sumit Bansal v. MGI Developers and Promoters
headline: Multiple Dishonoured Cheques From One Transaction Are Separate Causes of Action: Supreme Court
summary: The Supreme Court held that where multiple cheques issued in connection with a single underlying transaction are dishonoured on different dates and followed by separate statutory notices, each dishonoured cheque gives rise to a distinct, independent cause of action under Section 138 of the Negotiable Instruments Act, 1881 - multiple complaints arising from the same transaction are not, by that fact alone, an abuse of

case: Kaveri Plastics v. Mahdoom Bawa Bahrudeen Noorul
headline: A Demand Notice Must Match the Cheque Amount Exactly, or the Complaint Fails: Supreme Court
summary: The Supreme Court quashed a Section 138 Negotiable Instruments Act complaint where the statutory demand notice sought Rs. 2 crore although the dishonoured cheque was for Rs. 1 crore, holding that a demand notice must claim the exact cheque amount and that even this kind of discrepancy is fatal to the complaint's maintainability.

case: National Seeds Corporation Ltd. v. National Agro Seed Corporation (India)
headline: Depositing an Award Amount in Court Doesn't Stop Interest Unless the Deposit Is Unconditionally Withdrawable: Supreme Court
summary: A Bench of Justices P.S. Narasimha and Alok Aradhe held that an award-debtor's liability to pay interest does not cease merely because the award amount is deposited in court; interest liability ends only where the deposit is made in accordance with Order XXI Rule 1 CPC, so that the award-holder can withdraw it unconditionally. The Court affirmed the Delhi High Court's direction to pay 12% annual interest for the peri

case: Dhanbad Fuels Pvt. Ltd. v. Union of India & Anr.
headline: Rejection of a Commercial Suit for Skipping Section 12A Pre-Institution Mediation Applies Prospectively, From 20 August 2022
summary: The Supreme Court reconciled its earlier decisions and held that, while pre-institution mediation under Section 12A of the Commercial Courts Act, 2015 remains mandatory, the consequence of outright rejection of the plaint for non-compliance applies only to suits instituted on or after 20 August 2022; suits filed earlier without pre-institution mediation are to be kept in abeyance with mediation directed at that stage

case: M. Gagan Bothra v. Senthil Kumar
headline: Foreign Residence Is No Bar to a Section 95 IBC Petition Against a Personal Guarantor: NCLT Chennai
summary: Admitting a Section 95 IBC application against a personal guarantor who resisted the petition partly on the ground that he resided abroad, the NCLT Chennai Bench held the Code does not restrict its applicability to personal guarantors based on nationality or place of residence, particularly where the guarantee was executed with a Chennai address and the underlying corporate debtor was based in Chennai.

case: Pankaj Chhabildas Sheth v. Abhyudaya Co-Operative Bank Ltd.
headline: A Section 94 Personal Insolvency Plea Cannot Be Used to Stall SARFAESI Recovery: NCLAT
summary: Dismissing a personal guarantor's appeal, NCLAT upheld the NCLT's finding that his Section 94 IBC application was really an attempt to obtain an interim moratorium and obstruct the bank's lawful recovery and SARFAESI enforcement rather than a genuine bid at insolvency resolution, holding that such applications must be pursued in good faith for actual resolution, not as a shield against creditor enforcement.

case: Bhumika Nilay R. Shah & Ors. v. Prawincharan Prafulcharan Dwary & Ors.
headline: Personal Guarantors Cannot Reopen a Final DRT Liability Finding Through Section 114 IBC Proceedings: NCLAT
summary: Dismissing appeals by three personal guarantors of Archon Engicon Ltd., NCLAT held that because the Debt Recovery Tribunal's 2021 order upholding the guarantee and fixing joint and several liability for over Rs. 149.26 crore had attained finality and was never challenged, the guarantors could not re-agitate the extent of that liability in collateral proceedings under Section 114 of the IBC.

case: Duke Fashions (India) Ltd. & Anr. v. Pramod Kumar Misra (Liquidator of Venus Garments (India) Ltd.) & Ors.
headline: A Liquidator Can Recover Possession Through the NCLT Without Going to a Rent Controller: NCLAT
summary: Dismissing occupants' appeals against an NCLT eviction order, NCLAT held that a liquidator's recovery of a corporate debtor's premises does not convert the dispute into a landlord-tenant matter, so occupants cannot invoke state rent-control legislation, such as the East Punjab Urban Rent Restriction Act, 1949, to resist a liquidator's possession claim before the NCLT.

case: Satinder Singh Bhasin v. Col. Gautam Mullick & Ors. — (2026) ibclaw.in 47 SC
headline: 100-Allottee Threshold Under Section 7 Is Fixed at Date of Petition Registration
summary: The Supreme Court held that the statutory threshold of 100 allottees (or 10% of allottees) for a Section 7 petition by homebuyers is to be determined as on the date of registration of the petition, not at the date of hearing or admission, and that substitution of petitioners prior to registration is permissible under the NCLT Rules. Two intrinsically linked and jointly liable real estate companies could also be proce

case: Acute Daily Media v. Rockman Advertising — 2025 ibclaw.in 41 NCLAT
headline: CIRP Terminated and SCN Issued Under Section 65 IBC for Collusive, Malicious Application
summary: The NCLAT upheld the NCLT's termination of a CIRP and issuance of a show cause notice for penalty under Section 65 IBC after finding that the Section 7 application was filed collusively, with fabricated and antedated documents, for a purpose other than genuine insolvency resolution. The judgment reinforces the IBC's integrity safeguards against process misuse.

case: Avil Menezes (Liquidator) v. Hinduja Leyland Finance — 2025 ibclaw.in 55 NCLAT
headline: Consortium Lender Cannot Claim Priority Over Pre-Existing Charge Without NOC
summary: The NCLAT held that where a consortium of banks held a first pari-passu charge on a corporate debtor's assets, a lender who refinanced those assets after the prior charge had crystallised cannot claim a first charge without a No Objection Certificate from all consortium members. The ruling protects consortium lenders' security interests from unilateral refinancing.

case: SBI v. India Power Corporation — 2025 ibclaw.in 61 SC
headline: NCLT Cannot Ignore a Rejoinder Affidavit After It Has Already Condoned the Delay in Filing It
summary: The Supreme Court held that once the NCLT condones delay in filing a rejoinder affidavit, it cannot then direct that the factual assertions in the rejoinder be disregarded while deciding a Section 7 application. The condonation order, once granted, must result in full substantive consideration of the affidavit's contents.

case: Kalyani Transco v. Bhushan Power & Steel — 2025 SCC OnLine SC 1010
headline: JSW Steel Resolution Plan Set Aside — CIRP 330-Day Limit Violated; Liquidation Ordered
summary: The Supreme Court set aside JSW Steel's approved resolution plan for BPSL — previously cleared by NCLT and NCLAT — and ordered liquidation. The CIRP exceeded the mandatory 330-day limit under Section 12. Resolution Applicants must submit unconditional and immediately enforceable plans and must disclose Section 29A eligibility via affidavit. NCLT/NCLAT cannot review decisions of statutory bodies (such as the ED under

case: Independent Sugar Corporation v. Girish Sriram Juneja — 2025 ibclaw.in 37 SC
headline: CCI Approval Under Section 31(4) IBC Before CoC Resolution Plan Approval Is MANDATORY
summary: The Supreme Court reversed the NCLT and NCLAT in the Hindustan National Glass/AGI Greenpac CIRP, holding that the proviso to Section 31(4) IBC — requiring prior CCI clearance for resolution plans involving market-consolidating combinations — is mandatory, not directory. A CoC cannot approve a plan without CCI clearance where the plan creates a combination.

case: Visa Coke Ltd. v. Mesco Kalinga Steel — 2025 ibclaw.in 168 SC
headline: Service of Section 8 Demand Notice on KMP at Registered Office Constitutes Valid Service
summary: The Supreme Court held that service of an operational creditor's demand notice under Section 8 IBC upon the Key Managerial Personnel of the corporate debtor at its registered office constitutes valid service. Procedural defects should not defeat substantive rights where no real prejudice is demonstrated. The NCLT and NCLAT had dismissed the Section 9 petition on non-service grounds, which the Supreme Court reversed.

case: Tata Steel v. Raj Kumar Banerjee — 2025 SCC OnLine SC 1042
headline: NCLAT Cannot Condone Appeal Delay Beyond the Mandatory 45-Day Outer Limit Under Section 61(2)
summary: The Supreme Court set aside NCLAT's condonation of a 46-day appeal delay in the BPSL/Rohit Ferro-Tech CIRP, holding that the outer 45-day limit under Section 61(2) is an absolute bar. The NCLAT has no power — equitable or inherent — to condone delays beyond this limit. The IBC's timeliness framework cannot be diluted by procedural flexibility.

case: M/s Sunshine Builders v. HDFC Bank — CA No. 5290/2025
headline: Section 18 SARFAESI Pre-Deposit Is Not Mandatory for Procedural or Interim DRT Orders
summary: The Supreme Court held through purposive interpretation that the Section 18 SARFAESI pre-deposit condition is not triggered by every DRT order. Procedural or interim orders — such as rejection of delay condonation or impleadment applications — do not attract the pre-deposit requirement. Only substantive orders determining liability require pre-deposit.

case: Indian Bank v. M/s Aman Hospitality — 2025 ibclaw.in 27 NCLAT
headline: Power of Attorney by Officer's Designation (Not Name) Is Valid for IBC Filings
summary: The NCLAT held that a Power of Attorney executed by the General Manager of a bank by designation — rather than naming specific individuals — is valid for IBC proceedings. Technical objections challenging authority were rejected as obstructing justice. Banks may authorise branch-level officers by their designation for IBC applications.

case: M.S. Sanjay v. Indian Bank — 2025 INSC 177
headline: Mandatory 30-Day Gap Between SARFAESI Sale Notice Publication and Auction Under Rule 9
summary: The Supreme Court confirmed that the 30-day notice period between publication of the SARFAESI sale notice and the auction under Rule 9 of the Security Interest (Enforcement) Rules, 2002 is mandatory. Auctions conducted without observing this gap are void. The amended Rule 9(1) providing a 15-day period for re-auction does not apply retrospectively to auctions initiated under the prior rule.

case: Angelwoods Apartment Allottees Association v. M. Lalitha & Anr.
headline: An NCLAT Appeal Filed Without a Certified Copy of the NCLT Order Is Not Merely Defective — It Is Incompetent
summary: The Supreme Court held that an appeal filed before the NCLAT without a certified copy of the impugned NCLT order, and without an accompanying exemption application, is not a curable irregularity but is "wholly incompetent" in the eyes of law. On the facts, the appeal had been e-filed on the very last day of the 45-day outer limit under Section 61(2) of the IBC without the certified copy, and the subsequent delay-cond

case: Regional Provident Fund Commissioner-II v. Ms. Mamta Binani & Ors.
headline: An NCLAT Portal Glitch on the Last Day of Limitation Doesn't Cost You the Appeal: Supreme Court
summary: A Bench of Justices Dipankar Datta and Sheel Nagu restored an NCLAT appeal under Section 61(2) of the IBC that had been dismissed as time-barred, after the appellant's counsel made a bona fide attempt to e-file on the last day of limitation but could not because of a backend technical glitch in NCLAT's own e-filing portal, with the appeal actually filed only one day late. Invoking the principle that an act of the cou

case: Srinivasa Reddy Velagala v. Sravanthi Infratech Pvt. Ltd.
headline: A Subsisting Contract Doesn't Keep a Stale IBC Claim Alive Past Limitation: Supreme Court
summary: The Supreme Court held that a Section 9 IBC application based on an EPC contract for a 225 MW gas-based power station was time-barred, since the operational creditor's claims had crystallised around 2011-2012 but the insolvency application was filed only in 2018. The Court clarified that the mere subsistence of an underlying contract does not create a continuing cause of action or indefinitely extend limitation once

case: ASR Market Ventures Private Limited v. Fitship Private Limited & Anr.
headline: Occasional Use Alongside a House Mark Does Not Create Standalone Trademark Rights: Delhi High Court
summary: Dismissing FITPASS owner ASR Market Ventures' rectification petition against Fitship's registered FITFEAST mark and refusing an interim injunction, Justice Jyoti Singh held ASR's own records showed it had consistently promoted its business under the umbrella mark FITPASS, with only scant, non-source-identifying references to FITFEAST, so it failed to establish independent goodwill in that term.

case: Graviss Foods Private Limited v. Registrar of Trade Marks
headline: 'ICE CREAM ROCKS' Is Too Generic and Descriptive to Register as a Trademark: Bombay High Court
summary: Dismissing Baskin Robbins licensee Graviss Foods' challenge to the Registrar's refusal to register 'ICE CREAM ROCKS', Justice Somasekhar Sundaresan held the phrase lacked the distinctive character needed for registration under Sections 9(1)(a) and 9(1)(b) of the Trade Marks Act, 1999, being too generic and descriptive of the goods despite the brand's marketing use.

case: K. Mangayarkarasi v. N.J. Sundaresan — 2025 INSC 687 : (2025) 8 SCC 299
headline: Trademark Disputes Arising From Contractual Obligations (Assignment Deeds, Licences) Are Arbitrable
summary: The Supreme Court held that not all trademark disputes are non-arbitrable. Disputes in personam arising from contractual obligations under a trademark licence or assignment deed are arbitrable. Allegations of fraud or statutory violations do not preclude arbitration where the dispute stems from an arbitration agreement in the underlying contract. The referral court's role under Section 8 is limited to verifying the e

case: AbbVie Biotherapeutics v. Controller of Patents — 2025 SCC OnLine Del 2384
headline: Post-Filing Patent Claim Expansion Is Impermissible Under Section 59 of the Patents Act, 1970
summary: The Delhi High Court rejected AbbVie's post-filing amendment seeking to expand from a method-specific antibody claim to a broader product-level claim. The Court held that while Section 59 permits amendments to narrow or clarify the patent's scope, it cannot be used to transform the nature of the claimed invention from a method to a product patent.

case: Hoffmann-La Roche AG v. Natco Pharma — 2025 SCC OnLine Del 1826
headline: Interim Injunction Denied on Lifesaving SMA Drug Despite Valid Patent — Public Health Prevails
summary: The Delhi High Court denied Roche an interim injunction against Natco's generic version of Risdiplam (for Spinal Muscular Atrophy) despite Roche holding a granted Indian patent. The Court found a credible patentability challenge and, critically, balanced the public health need of SMA patients against patent protection — the access-to-medicine consideration tilted the balance of convenience against the patentee.

case: ITC Limited & Anr. v. Adyar Gate Hotels Limited
court: Supreme Court of India (dismissing SLP against Delhi High Court Division Bench order)
headline: Supreme Court Declines to Revive ITC's Injunction Against Adyar Gate Hotels' Use of the 'DAKSHIN' Mark
summary: ITC, which holds registrations for the 'DAKSHIN' mark since 2000 and had licensed Adyar Gate Hotels to use the name at its Chennai hotel from 1985, sued to restrain Adyar Gate from operating a standalone 'Dakshin' restaurant after the original hotel premises were demolished. After a single judge granted ITC an interim injunction, a Delhi High Court Division Bench set aside that injunction, finding no prima facie case

case: Sukhendu Bhattacharjee v. State of Assam
headline: Arbitrary Denial of Regularisation to Similarly Situated Workers Violates Article 14
summary: The Supreme Court reaffirmed the constitutional guarantee of equality, holding that the State of Assam could not arbitrarily deny regularisation benefits to a group of muster-roll and work-charged employees who were similarly situated to thousands of workers already regularised. Differential treatment among an otherwise homogenous class of long-serving employees was held to be unconstitutional.

case: Dushyant Janbandhu v. Hyundai Autoever India — 2024 SCC OnLine SC 3691
headline: Labour Disputes Including Non-Payment of Wages and Termination Are Non-Arbitrable
summary: The Supreme Court held that disputes relating to non-payment of wages and the legality of termination — governed by statutory labour authorities — are non-arbitrable. An employer cannot compel an employee to arbitrate these statutory labour rights even if the employment contract contains an arbitration clause.

case: M/s Kerala Industrial Infrastructure Development Corporation v. Central Board of Trustees & Anr.
headline: Is Maximum EPF Default Damages Mandatory or Discretionary? Supreme Court Refers the Question to a Larger Bench
summary: A Bench of Justices J.B. Pardiwala and K. Vinod Chandran, while resolving appeals over provident fund and gratuity dues owed to workmen in an insolvency-resolution context, referred to a larger Bench the question whether the authorised officer has discretion under Section 14B of the Employees' Provident Funds and Miscellaneous Provisions Act, 1952 to levy less than full damages for default, or whether imposition of m

case: Srinibas Goradia v. Arvind Kumar Sahu & Ors.
headline: A Managerial Job Title Doesn't Defeat Workman Status — the 'Dominant Nature of Duties' Test Decides: Supreme Court
summary: A cashier designated 'Front Office Manager' and later 'Executive' was terminated, and the High Court reversed the Labour Court's reinstatement award on the basis of his managerial designation. Justices Prashant Kumar Mishra and N.V. Anjaria restored the Labour Court's award, holding that the 'dominant nature of duties' test — not the employer's chosen designation — determines workman status under Section 2(s) of the

case: Sudhir & Ors. v. Head of Human Resource, Dainik Bhaskar Group (D.B. Corp. Ltd.) & Ors.
headline: A State Government Cannot Delegate Its Section 17(2) Power to Refer a Working Journalists' Dues Dispute: Supreme Court
summary: The Supreme Court held that while Section 17(1) of the Working Journalists and Other Newspaper Employees Act, 1955 expressly permits delegation of the State Government's recovery-certificate function, Section 17(2)'s power to refer a dues dispute to a Labour Court contains no such delegation clause, so a reference made by an Additional or Deputy Commissioner of Labour under a general delegation notification is not va

case: WP(C) — FSSAI Regulatory Inaction
court: Supreme Court — Bench of Justices Pardiwala & Mahadevan
headline: Supreme Court Issues 3-Month Ultimatum to FSSAI on Nutraceutical Rules and Front-of-Pack Labelling
summary: The Supreme Court issued a stern 3-month deadline to the Centre and FSSAI to notify pending food safety rules — particularly regarding front-of-pack nutrition labelling and regulation of health supplements and nutraceuticals (a ₹30,000 crore market with largely unregulated health claims). The Court emphasised urgency given the growing public health hazard from unsubstantiated product claims.

case: P B Agro LLP v. Union of India & Ors.
headline: Suing From Delhi or Naming FSSAI as a Party Doesn't Create Delhi Jurisdiction Over a State FDA Notice
summary: P B Agro LLP, master licensee of the VIMAL brand, filed a writ petition in Delhi after the Assistant Commissioner (Food), FDA Greater Mumbai, issued a show-cause notice under the Food Safety and Standards Act, 2006 to three of its brand ambassadors over an advertising campaign for its Elaichi and Pan Masala products; the petitioner argued Delhi jurisdiction on the basis that it operated from Delhi, paid the ambassado

case: Shivam Traders and Hire Purchase Pvt. Ltd. v. Madhusudan Vehicles Pvt. Ltd.
headline: Only the NCLT Can Restrain an NBFC's Premature Loan Recovery, Not a Civil Court: Allahabad High Court
summary: Dismissing a borrower's appeal seeking an injunction against an NBFC's premature recovery of a nine-year loan facility, the Allahabad High Court held that under Section 45QA of the RBI Act, 1934 read with Section 430 of the Companies Act, 2013, only the NCLT has jurisdiction over a dispute concerning premature repayment of a deposit or loan from an NBFC, and a civil court cannot grant an injunction restraining such r

case: Sandeep Kumar Bhagat v. Punjab National Bank & Ors.
headline: NCLT Cannot Force a Bank to Accept a One-Time Settlement, Even After Liquidation Has Begun
summary: Refusing to direct PNB to accept a Rs. 22.50 crore one-time settlement proposed by the legal heirs of a personal guarantor after three group companies were ordered into liquidation, the NCLT Guwahati Bench held that accepting an OTS proposal is a matter of commercial discretion for the lender, and the Tribunal has no power to compel a financial creditor to accept a settlement that was never crystallised into a bindin

case: Bank of India v. Sri Nangli Rice Mills — 2025 INSC 765
headline: Section 11 SARFAESI Creates Statutory Mandatory Arbitration for All Inter-Creditor Disputes
summary: The Supreme Court definitively held that Section 11 SARFAESI creates a statutory mandatory arbitration for all disputes between banks, financial institutions, ARCs, and qualified buyers involving securitisation, reconstruction, and non-payment of dues. No written arbitration agreement is required — the Act creates a statutory deemed consent. The DRT has no jurisdiction over such inter-creditor disputes.

case: M/s Sunshine Builders v. HDFC Bank — CA No. 5290/2025
headline: Section 18 SARFAESI Pre-Deposit Not Mandatory for Procedural/Interim DRT Orders
summary: The Supreme Court held through purposive interpretation that Section 18 SARFAESI's pre-deposit requirement is not triggered by procedural or interim DRT orders — such as rejection of delay condonation or impleadment applications. Only substantive orders determining liability attract the pre-deposit condition. This prevents mechanistic denial of appellate access for procedural challenges.

case: M.S. Sanjay v. Indian Bank — 2025 INSC 177
headline: 30-Day Gap Between SARFAESI Sale Notice Publication and Auction Is Mandatory Under Rule 9
summary: The Supreme Court confirmed that the 30-day notice period between publication of the SARFAESI sale notice and the auction under Rule 9 of the Security Interest (Enforcement) Rules, 2002 is mandatory and not directory. Auctions conducted without observing this gap are void. The amended Rule 9(1) providing a 15-day period for re-auction does not apply retrospectively.

case: Central Bank of India v. Prabha Jain — 2025 SCC OnLine SC 121
headline: Civil Courts Retain Jurisdiction Over Property Title Disputes Notwithstanding Active SARFAESI Enforcement
summary: The Supreme Court held that civil courts retain jurisdiction over property ownership and title disputes even during SARFAESI enforcement proceedings. The DRT's powers under Section 17 are strictly limited to examining the validity of Section 13(4) enforcement measures — it cannot adjudicate title or validity of pre-existing sale or mortgage deeds. The Court also directed RBI and banks to develop standardised Title Cl

case: Kotak Mahindra Bank Limited v. Trupti Sanjay Mehta & Ors.
headline: A Bank Can Use SARFAESI on Debt Assigned by an NBFC That Was Never Itself Covered by the Act: Supreme Court
summary: A Bench of Justices Sanjay Kumar and Sanjeev Sachdeva held that a bank can invoke the SARFAESI Act, 2002 to recover a secured loan it acquired by assignment from an NBFC, even though that NBFC was not a 'financial institution' covered by the Act at the time the loan was originally created, setting aside a Bombay High Court ruling that had restricted Kotak Mahindra Bank from enforcing SARFAESI against a loan portfolio

case: NBFC Scale Based Regulatory Framework — Upper Layer Compliance Timelines
headline: RBI Tightens Governance and Disclosure Timelines for Upper Layer NBFCs Under the Scale Based Regulatory Framework
summary: RBI has tightened compliance timelines for NBFCs classified in the 'Upper Layer' under its Scale Based Regulation framework, including enhanced board-level governance requirements, more frequent disclosure of asset quality and liquidity metrics, and a differentiated, bank-like regulatory capital treatment for the largest NBFCs in this category.

case: Procure Logistics Services Pvt. Ltd. v. Axis Bank Ltd.
headline: A Bank Cannot Cite Generalised Suspicion to Refuse Demonetised Deposits Into a KYC-Compliant Account: NCDRC
summary: Holding Axis Bank liable for deficiency in service, the NCDRC found that the bank's blanket refusal to accept demonetised currency deposits into a KYC-compliant current account, within the window the Government's November 2016 notification allowed, was not authorised by that notification, and directed the bank to pay the complainant Rs. 3.19 crore with 6% simple interest from December 2016.

case: RERA Pragati Review — PM Scrutiny
headline: PM Modi Scrutinises RERA at Pragati Meeting — Questions Whether 'Disposed' Means Real Relief
summary: At a Pragati meeting in 2026, Prime Minister Modi questioned whether RERA complaints marked 'disposed' actually result in compensation or possession for homebuyers. He urged states to ensure genuine relief delivery over mere statistical disposal counts, emphasising strict compliance with RERA rules.

case: State of Himachal Pradesh v. Naresh Sharma — SLP(C) 5835/2026
headline: Supreme Court Criticises RERA: 'Better to Abolish This Institution' if It Only Serves Defaulting Builders
summary: A bench of CJI Surya Kant and Justice Joymalya Bagchi issued strong observations questioning RERA's national effectiveness while considering an HP RERA office relocation matter. The Court observed that RERA authorities seem to serve defaulting builders rather than homebuyers — CJI Surya Kant stated it may be 'better to abolish this institution' if this continues.

case: GMADA v. Anupam Garg — 2025 INSC 808
headline: No Double Compensation in Homebuyer Claims — Contractual Interest and Loan Interest Cannot Both Be Awarded
summary: The Supreme Court held that homebuyer compensation must not result in double recovery. Where an allotment letter provides an 8% compound interest remedy on delay, consumer fora cannot additionally award interest on the buyer's home loan. The contractual interest already compensates the financial cost of the investment.

case: The Managing Director, KSRTC v. P. Chandramouli & Ors.
headline: Employer Group Insurance Payouts Cannot Be Deducted From Motor Accident Compensation: Supreme Court
summary: A Bench of Justices Pankaj Mithal and Prasanna B. Varale held that amounts received by the dependants of a deceased accident victim under an employer-provided group insurance scheme or other independent contractual/social-security benefit cannot be deducted from the compensation awarded under the Motor Vehicles Act, since such benefits arise from a separate contractual relationship with no requisite nexus to statutor

case: Canara Bank v. Kavita Chowdhary
headline: Bank's Failure to Present Deposited Cheques Within Their Validity Period Is Deficiency in Service: Supreme Court
summary: A customer deposited two cheques worth over Rs. 1.06 crore with Canara Bank, but the bank failed to present them for clearance within their validity period, so they were returned as stale. A Bench of Justices B.V. Nagarathna and Ujjal Bhuyan upheld the NCDRC's finding of deficiency in service, while reducing the compensation awarded from 10% to 6% of the cheque amount with interest.

case: Parsvnath Developers Ltd. v. Mohit Khirbat
headline: Statutory Power to Award Just Compensation for Deficient Housing Service Cannot Be Curtailed by a One-Sided Flat Buyer Agreement Clause
summary: Dismissing a developer's appeals against NCDRC compensation awards, the Supreme Court held that a consumer forum's power to award reasonable compensation for a deficiency in service is a statutory power that a restrictive, standard-form delay-compensation clause cannot override, and that a detailed mathematical loss calculation is not a precondition to a reasoned, proportionate award.

case: Fortune Resources and Properties LLP v. Y.P. Goel and Associates and Anr.
headline: Absence of a Written Allotment Agreement Does Not Oust RERA's Jurisdiction: Chhattisgarh High Court
summary: Dismissing a builder's appeal under Section 58 of RERA, the Court held that an 'aggrieved person' under Section 31 of the Act and Rule 35 is of wide amplitude, and the mere absence of a written allotment agreement does not by itself defeat RERA's jurisdiction over a complaint, even where the underlying booking was oral.

case: N. Balakrishnan v. Tamil Nadu Real Estate Regulatory Authority & Ors.
headline: TNRERA Cannot Adjudicate a Disputed Question of Title While Registering a Project: Madras High Court
summary: A Thiruneermalai resident who claimed ownership of land in Tambaram challenged TNRERA's registration of a rival developer's project over the same land. Justice D. Bharatha Chakravarthy held that TNRERA cannot adjudicate a disputed question of title while examining a project registration application, and that a party disputing ownership of the underlying land must approach the competent civil court instead.

case: AGM Notice Period and E-Voting Compliance Under Renewed Scrutiny
headline: AGM Notice Period and E-Voting Compliance Under Renewed Scrutiny
summary: Following a spate of shareholder complaints, the Registrar of Companies in several jurisdictions has begun issuing show-cause notices to companies that combined a shortened AGM notice period with inadequate documentation of the 95% consent required under Section 101, or that failed to keep the remote e-voting window open for the full prescribed period.

case: Madras Bar Association v. Union of India — 2025 INSC 1330
headline: SC Strikes Down Tribunals Reforms Act Provisions — Orders Constitution of National Tribunals Commission
summary: The Supreme Court in Madras Bar Association v. Union of India (2025 INSC 1330) struck down key provisions of the Tribunals Reforms Act, 2021, reiterating that executive dominance over tribunal appointments violates judicial independence. The Court ordered the constitution of a National Tribunals Commission. This directly affects NCLT, NCLAT, SAT, and other commercial tribunal appointment processes.

case: Vedanta Demerger — Scheme of Arrangement Scrutiny
headline: Vedanta's Six-Way Demerger Faces NCLT Scrutiny Over Minority Shareholder Consent and Disclosure
summary: Vedanta's proposed six-way demerger faced significant procedural challenges before the NCLT regarding adequacy of minority shareholder consent, disclosure requirements under the Companies Act, 2013, and compliance with fair treatment obligations to retail investors. NCLT scrutiny of complex multi-entity restructurings has intensified significantly.

case: M/s PVCON Engineering Co. v. CGST and Central Excise, Bhopal & Ors.
headline: Supreme Court Permits GSTAT Appeal Without Pre-Deposit Pending Ruling on Penalty-Only Appeals Tied to Pre-Amendment SCNs
summary: The Court issued notice on whether the mandatory pre-deposit for a penalty-only GSTAT appeal, effective from 1 October 2025, should be calculated by reference to the underlying show cause notice date or the date the appeal is filed — the assessee had received a penalty-only order pursuant to a July 2024 SCN. Pending the outcome, the assessee was permitted to file its appeal without the pre-deposit.

case: Spherion Solutions Private Limited v. Additional Commissioner Adjudication CGST Delhi North & Ors.
headline: ITC Blocked Under Rule 86A Cannot Satisfy the GST Appeal Pre-Deposit
summary: Ruling on a challenge to a GST DRC-07 summary demand order, a Bench of Justices Anil Kshetarpal and Shail Jain held that input tax credit blocked under Rule 86A of the CGST Rules remains legally unavailable for debit and so cannot be treated as 'payment' satisfying the mandatory pre-deposit for a GST appeal under Section 107(6) of the CGST Act — blocking merely immobilises credit, whereas Section 107(6) requires actu

case: M/s Goodluck India Limited & Anr. v. Union of India & Ors.
headline: Omission of Rule 96(10) Without a Saving Clause Applies to Every Pending IGST Refund Proceeding: Supreme Court
summary: Rule 96(10) of the CGST Rules, which had restricted exporters using concessional-duty inputs from claiming IGST refunds, was omitted from 8 October 2024 without a saving clause. A Bench of Justices J.B. Pardiwala and K. Vinod Chandran held that, absent a saving clause, the omission applies to every refund proceeding still pending on that date, effectively closing such proceedings in the exporters' favour.

case: Serum Institute of India Pvt. Ltd. v. Maharashtra Electricity Regulatory Commission & Anr.
headline: A Captive Generator Must Be Paid for Surplus Power the Grid Absorbed During an Open Access Restriction: APTEL
summary: Setting aside MERC's 2019 rejection of Serum Institute's compensation claim, APTEL directed MERC to determine the amount payable by the Maharashtra distribution licensee, together with carrying costs, for over 3.67 crore units of surplus wind energy that Open Access restrictions forced Serum Institute's 57.2 MW captive wind plants to inject into the state grid between April 2016 and March 2018 instead of delivering t

case: Kirloskar Ferrous Industries Ltd. & Anr. v. Union of India & Anr.
headline: Royalty, DMF and NMET Payments Can Be Included When Computing an Iron Ore Miner's Own Royalty Base: Supreme Court
summary: A Bench of Justices J.B. Pardiwala and K.V. Viswanathan upheld the constitutional validity of the Explanation to Rule 38 of the Mineral Concession Rules, 2016 and Rule 45(8)(a) of the Mineral Conservation and Development Rules, 2017, which require royalty, DMF and NMET payments to be included in the sale value used to compute the Average Sale Price of iron ore for royalty purposes. The Court rejected the argument tha

case: Manav Bhanot v. National Highway Authority of India
headline: Solatium and Interest on NH Act Land Acquisitions Follow the Date of the Original Compensation Determination, Not a Later Award
summary: In a National Highways Act land acquisition where the Competent Authority first determined compensation in July 2014, the Supreme Court held solatium, interest and interest on solatium are payable under the 1894 Land Acquisition Act rather than the 2013 Act, because the deciding date is the Competent Authority's Section 3G(1) determination — not the notification date or a later arbitral award. The Court directed the

case: CCPA proceedings against Flipkart, Amazon and JioMart
headline: E-Commerce Platforms Fined for Listing an Unregistered Agrochemical, Cannot Hide Behind 'Intermediary' Status: CCPA
summary: Acting on a complaint about online listings for 'Cyclosinone Herbicide', a chemical never cleared under the Insecticides Act, 1968, the CCPA held that Flipkart, Amazon and JioMart had facilitated the sale of an unregistered agrochemical and that marketing silent on its active ingredient amounted to a misleading advertisement and unfair trade practice. Rejecting the platforms' intermediary defence, it fined Flipkart a

case: Mahinder & Others v. Puran Singh
headline: Class-I Heirs Have a Preferential Right to Acquire Inherited Agricultural Land Before It Passes to Outsiders
summary: The Supreme Court reinforced the legislative intent behind Section 22 of the Hindu Succession Act, 1956, confirming that where inherited agricultural land is to be transferred, Class-I heirs enjoy a preferential right to acquire it ahead of any sale to an outside purchaser, protecting family land holdings from fragmentation via third-party sale.

case: Kavitha Kuruganti v. PepsiCo India Holdings Pvt. Ltd.
headline: Suing Farmers for Seed Infringement Doesn't Void a Plant Variety's Registration, and Farmers Keep Their Statutory Privilege: Supreme Court
summary: A Bench of Justices J.B. Pardiwala and K. Vinod Chandran declined to revoke PepsiCo India's registration of its FL 2027 (FC-5) potato variety, used for Lay's chips, under Section 34(h) of the Protection of Plant Varieties and Farmers' Rights Act, 2001, holding that having earlier sued (and then withdrawn suits against) Gujarat farmers for infringement did not itself justify revocation. The Court simultaneously held t

case: Agriculture Produce Market Committee, Deesa v. National Horticulture Board & Ors.
headline: Supreme Court Examines NABARD's Withdrawal of a Horticulture Cold-Storage Subsidy From an APMC
summary: The APMC at Deesa had received a Capital Investment Subsidy from the National Horticulture Board, routed through NABARD, for construction/expansion/modernisation of cold storage facilities for horticultural produce; NABARD later decided to withdraw the subsidy and recover the amount already disbursed, a decision the NHB upheld. A Single Judge had set aside the withdrawal and held the APMC entitled to the full subsidy

case: Lachchappa and Others v. Special Land Acquisition Officer, UKP, Bagalkot and Others
headline: Abnormal Delay Is No Bar to Land-Acquisition Compensation Parity Under the Same Notification: Supreme Court Invokes Article 142
summary: Farmers whose agricultural land in Mudhol Village, Bagalkot District was acquired under a 1999 notification sought the same enhanced compensation rate already awarded to other landowners under the identical notification, despite a long delay in pursuing their own claim. A Bench of Justices S.V.N. Bhatti and N.V. Anjaria invoked Article 142 to hold that abnormal delay in claiming compensation is not, by itself, a bar

case: Nayan Bhowmick v. Aparna Chakraborty
headline: Supreme Court Dissolves a Marriage Under Article 142 Solely on Account of Decades of Delayed Litigation
summary: The parties married in August 2000, but the marriage lasted barely a year before the wife left; a divorce suit filed in 2003 was decreed by the trial court on grounds of desertion in 2010, reversed by the Gauhati High Court in 2011, and remained pending before the Supreme Court for over a decade. Invoking Article 142 of the Constitution, the Court dissolved the marriage, holding that forcing a couple to remain legall

case: Nikhat Parveen @ Khusboo Khatoon v. Rafique @ Shillu
headline: An Unchallenged DNA Report Excluding Paternity Defeats a Child Maintenance Claim: Supreme Court
summary: The parties married in March 2016 and had a child in April 2016; after marital discord, the wife sought maintenance for the child under the Protection of Women from Domestic Violence Act, 2005, but an unchallenged DNA test report dated 8 May 2017 excluded the respondent as the child's biological father. Justices Sanjay Karol and N. Kotiswar Singh held that where an unchallenged DNA report conclusively excludes patern

case: Sonal Talpada v. Veerbhan Singh
headline: Fifteen Years of Separation and Persistent Refusal of Conjugal Relations Can Itself Be Mental Cruelty: Supreme Court
summary: Two medical professionals with no children had lived separately for nearly 15 years with no effort at reconciliation; the husband sought divorce under Section 13(1)(ia) of the Hindu Marriage Act, 1955 on the ground of mental cruelty, which the Family Court declined but the Rajasthan High Court granted. Justices Sanjay Karol and Augustine George Masih upheld the divorce, holding that a prolonged period of separation,

case: Deepa Joshi v. Gaurav Joshi
headline: Loan Repayments Made Toward Asset Creation Cannot Be Equated With Necessary Expenditure to Dilute the Primary Duty to Maintain a Spouse
summary: In a maintenance proceeding under Section 144 of the Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita, 2023, the Supreme Court held that a husband's loan repayments directed toward building or acquiring an asset represent a form of personal investment and cannot be treated on the same footing as necessary subsistence expenditure, so as to substantially reduce the maintenance payable to a spouse without independent means.
